When we have an inequality involving an exponential function with a positive base, we're allowed to multiply or divide both sides by the exponential function.

Multiplying both sides of the given inequality by $(0.6)^{3x-2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{({x}^{2}-4)^{3}}{(0.6)^{3x-2}} & <0 \\ (0.6)^{3x-2}\cdot \frac{({x}^{2}-4)^{3}}{(0.6)^{3x-2}} & <(0.6)^{3x-2}\cdot 0 \\ ({x}^{2}-4)^{3} & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve the inequality using familiar methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{({x}^{2}-4)^{3}} & <\sqrt[3]{0} \\ {x}^{2}-4 & <0 \\ {x}^{2} & <4 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & <\sqrt{4} \\ |x| & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the inequality is $-2<x<2.$
